"when the last was seen": "the last" marks the end of the stay. It is not a printed number or quantity, so count is null.

quote: I found a nest with one egg on
why: "I found a nest with one egg" is a breeding note. No birds are seen or counted, and "one egg" is not a count of birds.
"first seen en rock": the birds are on the rock, and the rules count resting on a rock as settled
"leaving rock" is a departure, not birds flying past or migrating, so seen
"seen daily" says how often, not what time of day

quote:
They left on 2nd 
March, 1885
why: "They left on 2nd March, 1885" is a dated departure record for the Black-billed Auks, and reading 2 has nothing for it
"four from N.E. alighted in river": birds flying in with a direction; a river isn't the station, so not settled
'these birds come on the rock' means they alight on the rock, so settled.
'it is some time during the night that these birds come on the rock'

quote: 28th, ditto.
why: 'May 20th, hundreds of Puffins; 28th, ditto.' The 28th is a separate dated sighting, same as the 20th, so same_as fits.
"several about ship daily": 'daily' says how often, not what time of day
"31st, ditto" repeats "hundreds of"; copy it as printed
"31st, ditto, on rock, went §.": 'ditto' carries the count forward
"about twenty, all day; 93rd, ditto": ditto stands for the count, copied as printed
"always to be seen": "always" says how often, not what time of day, so time stays null
"is always here": "always" says how often, not what time of day

why: "six to twelve breed" is its own count of breeding birds, apart from "Six to one hundred frequent island"

why: "One to nine noted from 22nd August to Sept. 8th." is a sentence of its own; "all flying about ship" belongs to the next sentence (end of September, Oct. 9th and 10th), so for these birds only "noted" is stated.
"June 3rd to the 10th, ditto." gives no count words of its own. "several" stands only in the earlier sentence, outside this quote, and the count must appear in the quote.

quote: March 4th, 7th, and April 7th, some going N.W.
why: "March 4th, 7th, and April 7th, some going N.W." lists three separate dates. The 7th is its own sighting of Gannets passing N.W., and the readers agree on the shared March 4th observation, so neither seems to carry this date in other_dates.

June 19th
why: "Eggs taken on June 19th" records eggs, not birds seen. No bird behaviour from the rule list fits; arrival is already covered by the May 18th entry.

"arrival" only; don't infer passing
